topic: Interval Scheduling, Merging, and Greedy Optimization

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

examples.explanation: Since intervals [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, merge them into [1,6].
Intervals [1,4] and [4,5] touch at boundary 4 and are considered overlapping.
Interval [0,4] completely encompasses [1,4].
[2,3] is strictly inside [1,4], so merged interval remains [1,4].

commonMistakes: Failing to sort intervals by start time before merging
Overlooking fully enclosed intervals where curr[1] < last[1]
hints: Sort intervals by their starting times.
Iterate through sorted intervals: if current interval overlaps with previous merged one, extend previous merged interval's end.
Otherwise, append current interval as a new disjoint interval.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.statement:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]` sorted in ascending order by `start_i`. You are also given an interval `newInterval = [start, end]`.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that `intervals` is still sorted in ascending order and contains no overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

examples.explanation: Because the new interval [2,5] overlaps with [1,3], merge them into [1,5].
The new interval [4,8] overlaps with [3,5],[6,7],[8,10], merging into [3,10].
Inserting into empty list results in list containing just the new interval.
New interval is strictly to the right without any overlap.

commonMistakes: Not advancing the index properly across 3 stages (before, overlapping, after)
Mutating input array in-place causing index shifting bugs
hints: Divide intervals into three stages: strictly before newInterval, overlapping with newInterval, and strictly after.
Add all intervals ending before newInterval starts directly.
Merge overlapping intervals into newInterval by updating min start and max end.
Append the merged interval and all remaining intervals.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.statement:
Given an array of intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

Note that intervals which touch at a point are non-overlapping (e.g. `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` do not overlap).

examples.explanation: [1,3] can be removed and the rest of the intervals are non-overlapping.
You need to remove two [1,2] to leave one [1,2].
You don't need to remove any of the intervals since they are already non-overlapping.
Removing [1,100] and [2,12] leaves [1,11] and [11,22].

commonMistakes: Sorting by start time without handling end times greedily
Treating touching endpoints (start === end) as an overlap when problem allows touching
hints: This is equivalent to finding the maximum number of mutually compatible intervals (Interval Scheduling).
Greedily select intervals that finish earliest (sort by end time).
The number of intervals to remove equals total intervals minus the maximum non-overlapping set.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.statement:
Given an array of meeting time intervals where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, determine if a person could attend all meetings without overlapping.

Touching meetings (e.g. one ends at 10 and next starts at 10) do not overlap.

parameterDefinitions.name: intervals
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of meeting start and end times

examples.explanation: [0,30] conflicts with both [5,10] and [15,20].
Sorted: [2,4] and [7,10] do not overlap.
[4,9] and [4,17] overlap.
No meetings means no conflicts.

commonMistakes: Using <= instead of < for overlap when touching is permitted
Not sorting before checking adjacent intervals
hints: Sort meetings by start time.
Check whether any meeting starts before the prior meeting ends.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.statement:
Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required.

A room can be used immediately after a meeting ends if the next meeting starts at that exact same time.

examples.explanation: Room 1 hosts [0,30]. Room 2 can host [5,10] and [15,20] sequentially.
Meetings do not overlap, so 1 room suffices.
[1,4] and [2,5] overlap, requiring 2 rooms. [7,9] can reuse one of them.
Endpoints touch consecutively without overlap, requiring only 1 room.

commonMistakes: Counting overlapping pairs rather than concurrent active intervals
Not considering that meetings can be chained in the same room when start >= previous end
hints: Notice that a room is required whenever a meeting starts before the earliest ending meeting finishes.
Sort start times and end times separately.
Advance start pointer and increment rooms needed; when start >= earliest end, advance end pointer.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.statement:
There are spherical balloons taped to a flat wall represented by the XY-plane. For each balloon, you are given a 2D integer array `points` where `points[i] = [x_start, x_end]` represents a balloon whose horizontal diameter stretches between `x_start` and `x_end`.

An arrow can be shot up exactly vertically from different points along the x-axis. A balloon with `[x_start, x_end]` is burst by an arrow shot at `x` if `x_start <= x <= x_end`. Return the minimum number of arrows that must be shot to burst all balloons.

examples.explanation: Shoot arrow at x = 6 (bursting [2,8] and [1,6]) and x = 11 (bursting [10,16] and [7,12]).
No balloons overlap, so 4 separate arrows are required.
Shoot at x = 2 (bursts [1,2],[2,3]) and x = 4 (bursts [3,4],[4,5]).
Extreme 32-bit signed integers require 2 arrows.

commonMistakes: Integer overflow subtraction `a[1] - b[1]` when values are near 32-bit integer limits
Shooting arrow at start coordinate instead of greedy end coordinate
hints: Sort the balloons by their end coordinate.
Greedily shoot an arrow at the end coordinate of the first unburst balloon.
Any subsequent balloon starting at or before this arrow position will be burst simultaneously.

problems.title: Assign Cookies
problems.statement:
Assume you are an awesome parent and want to give your children some cookies. But, you should give each child at most one cookie.

Each child `i` has a greed factor `g[i]`, which is the minimum size of a cookie that the child will be content with; and each cookie `j` has a size `s[j]`. If `s[j] >= g[i]`, we can assign the cookie `j` to the child `i`, and the child `i` will be content. Your goal is to maximize the number of your content children and output the maximum number.

examples.explanation: Only child 1 (greed 1) can be content with cookie size 1.
Both children can be content.
No cookie is large enough for any child.
Cookies 7 and 8 satisfy children with greed 7 and 8.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N + M log M)
commonMistakes: Assigning a large cookie to a child with tiny greed when a smaller cookie would satisfy them
Not sorting both arrays before applying two pointers
hints: Greedily satisfy the least greedy children with the smallest possible sufficient cookie.
Sort both `g` and `s` in ascending order.
Advance cookie pointer on every step; advance child pointer only when satisfied.

problems.title: Lemonade Change
problems.statement:
At a lemonade stand, each lemonade costs `$5`. Customers are standing in a queue to buy from you and order one at a time. Each customer will only buy one lemonade and pay with either a `$5`, `$10`, or `$20` bill. You must provide the correct change to each customer so that the net transaction is that the customer pays `$5`.

Note that you do not have any change in hand at first. Return `true` if you can provide every customer with the correct change, or `false` otherwise.

parameterDefinitions.name: bills
parameterDefinitions.description: Sequence of bills paid by customers

examples.explanation: Collect 3 $5 bills. Give $5 change for the $10 bill. Give $10 + $5 change for the $20 bill.
For the two $10 bills we give two $5 bills. For the $20 bill we only have a $10 bill and no $5 bills left, so we cannot make $15 change.
Give three $5 bills as change for the $20 bill.
First customer pays $10 with zero change available.

commonMistakes: Giving three $5 bills instead of one $10 and one $5 when giving change for $20 (keeping $5 bills is more versatile)
Tracking $20 bills which can never be used as change
hints: Count only $5 and $10 bills because $20 bills can never be used as change.
For a $10 bill, you must return a $5 bill.
For a $20 bill, prefer giving $10 + $5 over three $5s, because $5 bills are strictly more flexible.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position.

Return `true` if you can reach the last index, or `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
You will always arrive at index 3 no matter what. Its maximum jump length is 0, making reaching the end impossible.
Already at the last index.
Jump 2 steps directly to last index.

commonMistakes: Continuing loop past the point where current index exceeds max reachable index
Overcomplicating with dynamic programming when a single greedy reach tracker is O(1) space
hints: Maintain the furthest index `maxReach` you can visit so far.
If you reach an index `i` that is greater than `maxReach`, you are stuck.
If `maxReach >= n - 1`, return true.

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.statement:
You are given a 0-indexed array of integers `nums` of length `n`. You are initially positioned at `nums[0]`.

Each element `nums[i]` represents the maximum length of a forward jump from index `i`. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach `nums[n - 1]`. The test cases are generated such that you can always reach `nums[n - 1]`.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
Jump from index 0 to 1, then jump to last index.
Jump from 0 to 1, then 1 to 2.
Already at last index, 0 jumps needed.

commonMistakes: Iterating up to `nums.length - 1` inclusive when deciding to make a jump, which adds an unnecessary jump
Using BFS / DP creating unnecessary O(N) space or O(N^2) time
hints: Think of this as BFS by levels where each level is the range of indices reachable with `k` jumps.
Track `curEnd` (boundary of current jump) and `curFarthest` (furthest index reachable for next jump).
When `i` reaches `curEnd`, you must take another jump, updating `curEnd = curFarthest`.

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.statement:
There are `n` gas stations along a circular route, where the amount of gas at the `i-th` station is `gas[i]`.

You have a car with an unlimited gas tank and it costs `cost[i]` of gas to travel from the `i-th` station to its next `(i + 1)-th` station. You begin the journey with an empty tank at one of the gas stations.

Given two integer arrays `gas` and `cost`, return the starting gas station's index if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction, otherwise return `-1`. If there exists a solution, it is guaranteed to be unique.

parameterDefinitions.name: cost
parameterDefinitions.description: Cost to travel to next station

examples.explanation: Start at station 3 (index 3). Fill with 4 gas, cost 1 -> tank 3. At station 4, add 5, cost 2 -> tank 6. At 0, add 1, cost 3 -> tank 4. At 1, add 2, cost 4 -> tank 2. At 2, add 3, cost 5 -> tank 0. Back at station 3!
Total gas 9 < total cost 10, impossible to complete circuit.
Single station with gas equal to cost.
Index 4 allows successfully completing the loop.

commonMistakes: Simulating starting from every index O(N^2) resulting in TLE
Not realizing that if sum(gas) < sum(cost), it is mathematically impossible to complete the loop
hints: If total gas is less than total cost, completing the circuit is impossible.
If you run out of gas between station `A` and station `B`, then no station between `A` and `B` can be the starting station.
Reset current tank and set `start = i + 1` whenever `currTank < 0`.

problems.title: Hand of Straights
problems.statement:
Alice has some number of cards and she wants to rearrange the cards into groups so that each group is of size `groupSize`, and consists of `groupSize` consecutive cards.

Given an integer array `hand` where `hand[i]` is the value written on the `i-th` card and an integer `groupSize`, return `true` if she can rearrange the cards, or `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Alice can rearrange the cards into [1,2,3], [2,3,4], [6,7,8].
Alice cannot rearrange the cards into groups of 4.
Cards are not consecutive.
Group size of 1 is always trivially satisfied.

commonMistakes: Forgetting early return `hand.length % groupSize !== 0`
Decrementing count one card at a time rather than batching by `c` leading to slower executions
hints: If `hand.length % groupSize !== 0`, immediately return false.
Count card frequencies with a hash map.
Sort the unique cards. The smallest remaining card must be the start of a consecutive group of length `groupSize`.

problems.title: Partitioning Into Minimum Number Of Deci-Binary Numbers
problems.statement:
A decimal number is called deci-binary if each of its digits is either `0` or `1` without any leading zeros. For example, `101` and `1100` are deci-binary, while `112` and `3001` are not.

Given a string `n` that represents a positive decimal integer, return the minimum number of positive deci-binary numbers needed so that they sum up to `n`.
constraints: n does not contain any leading zeros and represents a positive integer

examples.explanation: 10 + 11 + 11 = 32. Max digit is 3.
Max digit is 8, which requires at least 8 deci-binary numbers.
Max digit is 9.
1 is already deci-binary.

commonMistakes: Attempting arithmetic big-integer operations instead of inspecting individual digit maximums
Converting very large strings into BigInt or Number causing precision errors
hints: Each deci-binary number contributes at most 1 to any given digit place.
To form a digit `d` at any position, you need at least `d` deci-binary numbers.
The answer is simply the maximum digit present in `n`.

problems.title: Maximum Units on a Truck
problems.statement:
You are assigned to put some amount of boxes onto one truck. You are given a 2D array `boxTypes`, where `boxTypes[i] = [numberOfBoxes_i, numberOfUnitsPerBox_i]`:
- `numberOfBoxes_i` is the number of boxes of type `i`.
- `numberOfUnitsPerBox_i` is the number of units in each box of the type `i`.

You are also given an integer `truckSize`, which is the maximum number of boxes that can be put on the truck. You can choose any boxes to put on the truck as long as the number of boxes does not exceed `truckSize`.

Return the maximum total number of units that can be put on the truck.

parameterDefinitions.name: truckSize
parameterDefinitions.description: Maximum capacity in number of boxes

examples.explanation: Take 1 box with 3 units, 2 boxes with 2 units, and 1 box with 1 unit: 1*3 + 2*2 + 1*1 = 8 units.
Truck cannot carry any boxes.
All 3 boxes fit: 3 * 5 = 15 units.

problems.suboptimalTimeComplexity: O(M log M) where M = sum(boxes)
commonMistakes: Sorting by box count instead of units per box
Expanding all boxes into an array causing Memory Limit Exceeded
hints: Sort boxes in descending order of units per box (Fractional Knapsack greedy choice).
Pick as many boxes of the highest-yield type as fit into the remaining truck capacity.

problems.title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
problems.statement:
You are given an array of people, `people`, which are the attributes of some people in a queue (not necessarily in order). Each `people[i] = [h_i, k_i]` represents the `i-th` person of height `h_i` with exactly `k_i` other people in front who have a height greater than or equal to `h_i`.

Reconstruct and return the queue that is represented by the input array `people`. The returned queue should be formatted as an array `queue`, where `queue[j] = [h_j, k_j]` is the attributes of the `j-th` person in the queue (`queue[0]` is the person at the front of the queue).
constraints: It is guaranteed that the queue can be reconstructed.

examples.explanation: Person [5,0] has 0 people taller/equal in front. Person [7,0] has 0. Person [5,2] has [5,0] and [7,0] in front, etc.
Valid reconstruction matching each individual's k constraint.
Person [2,0] is in front, person [1,1] has 1 person taller in front.
Single person queue.

commonMistakes: Sorting ascending by height which makes subsequent insertions disrupt previous k counts
Sorting identical heights with wrong tiebreaker (must sort ascending by k for same height)
hints: Sort people by height descending.
For people of the same height, sort by `k` ascending.
Insert each person into the output array at index `k`. Since all previously placed people are taller, inserting at index `k` precisely satisfies their requirement.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.statement:
Given a characters array `tasks`, representing the tasks a CPU needs to do, where each letter represents a different task. Tasks could be done in any order. Each task is done in one unit of time. For each unit of time, the CPU could complete either one task or just be idle.

However, there is a non-negative integer `n` that represents the cooldown period between two same tasks (the same letter in the array), that is that there must be at least `n` units of time between any two same tasks.

Return the least number of units of times that the CPU will take to finish all the given tasks.

examples.explanation: A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B. Total 8 units.
With cooldown 0, no idle time is needed. Total 6 units.
Task A dominates: A -> B -> C -> A -> D -> E -> A -> F -> G -> A -> idle -> idle -> A -> idle -> idle -> A.
Single task takes 1 unit.

commonMistakes: Simulating unit-by-unit when mathematical slot calculation is O(1) space and O(N) time
Ignoring that `tasks.length` is a lower bound when idle time is negative
hints: Find the maximum frequency `maxFreq` of any task.
Count how many tasks share this maximum frequency `maxCount`.
The minimal layout structure has `(maxFreq - 1)` chunks of size `(n + 1)` plus `maxCount` tasks in the final chunk.
The answer is `max(tasks.length, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCount)`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=600 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Candy
problems.statement:
There are `n` children standing in a line. Each child is assigned a rating value given in the integer array `ratings`.

You are giving candies to these children subjected to the following requirements:
1. Each child must have at least one candy.
2. Children with a higher rating get more candies than their neighbors.

Return the minimum number of candies you need to have to distribute the candies to the children.

examples.explanation: Distribute candies: [2,1,2].
Distribute candies: [1,2,1]. The third child has rating 2, which is not strictly higher than rating 2 of neighbor.
Distribute candies: [1,2,1,2,1].
Single child gets 1 candy.

commonMistakes: Doing only a single left-to-right pass, missing right-to-left downward slopes
Giving more candies when neighbors have equal ratings (equal ratings don't require strictly more candies)
hints: Satisfy the two neighbor conditions separately using two passes.
Left-to-right pass: if `ratings[i] > ratings[i-1]`, set `candies[i] = candies[i-1] + 1`.
Right-to-left pass: if `ratings[i] > ratings[i+1]`, update `candies[i] = max(candies[i], candies[i+1] + 1)`.

problems.title: Video Stitching
problems.statement:
You are given a series of video clips from a sporting event that lasted `time` seconds. These video clips can be represented with an array of clips where `clips[i] = [start_i, end_i]`.

We can cut these clips into segments freely. Return the minimum number of clips needed so that we can cut the clips into a list of segments to cover the entire sporting event `[0, time]`. If the task is impossible, return `-1`.

parameterDefinitions.name: time
parameterDefinitions.description: Total duration to cover from 0 to time

examples.explanation: Clips only cover up to time 2, cannot reach 5.
Single clip covers [0,5] completely.

commonMistakes: Not returning -1 when no clip starts at 0 or when a gap exists
Allowing intervals that start after `curEnd` without properly triggering the next segment
hints: Transform this into Jump Game II: for each time `t`, what is the furthest reach of a clip starting at `t`?
Greedily pick the clip that extends coverage the furthest while overlapping current covered range.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Move Chips to The Same Position
problems.statement:
We have `n` chips. The position of the `i-th` chip is `position[i]`.

We want to move all the chips to the same position. In one step, we can change the position of the `i-th` chip from `position[i]` to:
- `position[i] + 2` or `position[i] - 2` with cost = 0.
- `position[i] + 1` or `position[i] - 1` with cost = 1.

Return the minimum cost needed to move all the chips to the same position.

examples.explanation: Move chip at pos 3 to pos 1 (cost 0). Move chip at pos 2 to pos 1 (cost 1). Total cost = 1.
Move two chips at 3 to pos 2 with cost 1 each. Total cost = 2.
Odd position 1 to even position 10^9 costs 1.
All chips are at even positions, moving by steps of 2 costs 0.

commonMistakes: Simulating movements coordinate by coordinate
Overlooking parity invariance: moving by 2 preserves parity for free; only changing parity costs 1
hints: Notice moving by 2 costs 0. That means all even numbers can be gathered at 0 for free, and all odd numbers can be gathered at 1 for free.
Moving between an even position and an odd position costs 1.
The answer is simply `min(evenCount, oddCount)`.

problems.title: Wiggle Subsequence
problems.statement:
A wiggle sequence is a sequence where the differences between successive numbers strictly alternate between positive and negative. The first difference (if one exists) may be either positive or negative. A sequence with one element and a sequence with two non-equal elements are trivially wiggle sequences.

Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest wiggle subsequence of `nums`.

A subsequence is obtained by deleting some elements (possibly zero) from the original sequence, leaving the remaining elements in their original order.

examples.explanation: Differences: (6, -3, 5, -7, 3) alternate signs. Entire sequence is wiggle.
Subsequence [1, 17, 10, 13, 10, 16, 8] achieves wiggle length 7.
Any two distinct elements give length 2.
Equal elements cannot alternate, longest wiggle is 1.

commonMistakes: Handling consecutive identical numbers as transitions
Overcomplicating with O(N^2) DP when greedy peak/valley tracking is O(N) time and O(1) space
hints: Think of this geometrically as finding local extrema (peaks and valleys).
Maintain `up` (length of wiggle ending with positive diff) and `down` (length of wiggle ending with negative diff).
If `nums[i] > nums[i-1]`, `up = down + 1`. If `nums[i] < nums[i-1]`, `down = up + 1`.

problems.title: Maximum Length of Pair Chain
problems.statement:
You are given an array of `n` pairs `pairs` where `pairs[i] = [left_i, right_i]` and `left_i < right_i`.

A pair `p2 = [c, d]` follows a pair `p1 = [a, b]` if `b < c`. A chain of pairs can be formed in this fashion.

Return the length longest chain which can be formed. You do not need to use up all the given intervals. You can select pairs in any order.

examples.explanation: Longest chain is [1,2] -> [3,4] of length 2.
Single pair chain has length 1.

commonMistakes: Sorting by left endpoint instead of right endpoint for greedy selection
Using >= instead of > for pair chain condition (problem requires `b < c`)
hints: This is identical to the interval scheduling problem.
Sort pairs by their second coordinate (finish time).
Greedily select the pair that finishes earliest to leave the maximum room for remaining pairs.
